note.note:
History:
- Presenting complaint: Wheeze and shortness of breath starting 2 days ago after cleaning the house and heavy dust exposure.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began approximately 1 hour after exposure, have persisted for 2 days, and have been worse at night; patient reports progressive worsening and is particularly worried today.
- Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath significant enough that patient sometimes cannot complete sentences when talking. No chest pain with deep breaths. No dizziness or vertigo.
- Treatments tried: None for current episode.
- Context/triggers/previous episodes: Childhood asthma (mostly resolved), occasional exercise-induced wheeze, seasonal hay fever in summer. Patient believes she may be dust-allergic.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma in childhood; intermittent exertional symptoms as adult.
- Seasonal hay fever (summer).
- Medications:
  - Inhaler reported to be available from a couple of months ago — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Prior systemic steroids for asthma in the past — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: Patient reports "not that I know of" (no known drug allergies documented).
- Regular care: Does not see a doctor regularly for asthma.
- Social/access: GP surgery is a few minutes' drive away.

Physical Examination:
- No in-person physical examination documented in the transcript.
- Reported/observed findings:
  - Audible wheeze reported by patient.
  - Shortness of breath with speech limitation (unable to complete sentences at times).
  - No chest pain on deep inspiration.
  - No dizziness reported.
  - Oral intake/hydration: reports drinking ~4–5 glasses of water per day.
- No objective vitals, oxygen saturation, lung auscultation, or other exam findings documented.

Impression:
- Probable asthma exacerbation versus allergic bronchospasm triggered by dust exposure.

Management Plan:
- Immediate actions advised:
  - Patient advised to attend an in-person clinic/GP for assessment, including pulse oximetry (finger oximeter) and further testing to distinguish asthma vs allergy.
  - Trial of an oral antihistamine for suspected allergic component was recommended if available (patient currently has none at home). Antihistamine can be obtained over the counter or prescribed by GP.
  - Possible need for systemic corticosteroids was discussed; decision contingent on in-person assessment and test results.
  - GP letter to be written and sent via the app to notify primary care and facilitate in-person review.
- Practical advice:
  - Bring available inhaler to the GP appointment.
  - Attend GP promptly (clinic visit expected to take ~10 minutes).
- No prescriptions/medication doses administered during this consult.

Patient Summary:
- Patient with prior childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever developed wheeze and progressive shortness of breath over 2 days after heavy dust exposure while cleaning. The working consideration is an asthma exacerbation or allergic reaction; patient was advised to go to a clinic/GP for pulse oximetry and further assessment. An OTC antihistamine was suggested and systemic steroids may be required pending in-person evaluation.

Key Takeaways:
- Attend GP/clinic promptly for pulse oximetry and in-person assessment.
- Take an oral antihistamine if available/obtainable en route or via GP.
- Bring any inhaler to the appointment; systemic steroids may be prescribed if indicated after assessment.

Next Steps:
- In-person GP/clinic visit for pulse oximetry and respiratory examination.
- Possible investigations/treatments at visit: oxygen saturation measurement, lung auscultation, peak flow/spirometry as indicated, initiation of inhaled bronchodilator and/or systemic corticosteroids if exam/oxygenation warrants.
- Follow-up with GP after assessment; review of medication needs and asthma action plan if diagnosis confirmed.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No vital signs documented (respiratory rate, heart rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, temperature).
  - No objective respiratory exam findings (lung auscultation) or peak flow/spirometry results.
  - Details of the inhaler (type, dose, route, frequency) not documented.
  - Details of prior systemic steroid courses (dose, route, timing) not documented.
  - Smoking status, pregnancy status, and complete medication list not documented.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - None identified. (Patient states she "might have" an inhaler from a couple of months ago; no direct contradiction.)
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally understandable; occasional hesitations and brief loss of video signal were noted but did not prevent extraction of key clinical information.
